Unlock the full potential of your beef with this step-by-step method to achieve a restaurant-quality crust.

Start by lightly toasting chiles in a dry, heavy skillet over medium heat for just 30 seconds on each side, until fragrant but not blackened. Transfer to a plate and set aside.

More commonly, the text has been linked to the fact that Christian Spain had been conquered and occupied by Muslims. Anyone reading the official Royal Society report on the Krakatoa sunsets (published in 1888) will find flights of poetic prose rivaling those of Hopkins himself. Treatment for PTSD is a deeply personalized journey, tailored to the unique needs of every patient. It hinges on the severity of the diagnosis, the specific type of trauma—whether acute, chronic, or delayed—and its underlying causes.

The standard approach involves a combination of psychotherapy and medication. However, current evidence strongly supports Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) as the most effective intervention. Despite its proven superiority over medication, a critical barrier exists: the availability of qualified therapists varies dramatically across countries and even between cities.

Today, we are settled in our own home. Having cleared approximately five-and-twenty acres of land and constructed a sturdy house, our situation is now very agreeable. However, our journey to this haven was far from smooth.

When we first arrived to live in the bush, the area was sparsely populated. Aside from our own family, there were only two or three other settlers nearby, and no roads had been cut out for us. The only viable path to bring supplies from the nearest town lay on the opposite side of the water. Crossing this water required a log ferry or a birch-bark canoe.

The wooden log ferry was a large pine-log hollowed out by axes to accommodate three or four people. It was flat-bottomed and incredibly narrow, making it the primary mode of transport on these shallow waters.

For the water crossing, we utilized the birch-bark canoe. Made from sheets of birch bark, these vessels were ingeniously fashioned and sewn together by the Indians using the tough roots of cedar, young pine, or larch (tamarack). These crafts were exceptionally light, allowing them to be easily carried by just two people, or even by a single individual.

These were our ferry-boats, and they were quite frail, requiring great skill to manage. They were worked in the water using paddles, operated either kneeling or standing. The squaws were masterful in canoe management, preserving their balance with admirable skill while standing up to propel the little bark with great velocity through the water.

September is a quiet month, but October 11 marks the grand close of the harvest season with the **Meditrinalia**, a solemn ceremony resembling a modern Thanksgiving. On this day, the first of the new vintage and the wine of the old were tasted with ritual precision, believed to ward off disease.

However, historians agree that in its earliest origins, the god concerned was **Juppiter**.

Consequently, the song no longer elicits the same emotional responses from Swiss listeners today; having lost their original taste for simplicity, they can no longer regret its loss when reminded of it. But it is from habit, recollections, and a thousand circumstances retraced in this tune by those natives who hear it, and reminding them of their country, former pleasures of their youth, and all those ways of living, which occasion a bitter reflection at having lost them. ai_draft: Around the time William Peter Pepys was poking the painting of Verelst, the Dutch and Flemish artist Cornelis Norbertus Gijsbrechts was also causing confusion with the brush, creating his masterpiece known as *The Reverse of a Framed Painting* (ca. 1670), an image that, to modern eyes at least, remains his most striking. Gijsbrechts was a master of trompe l'oeil, the technique of painting in which the artist tricks the viewer into perceiving that they are looking at an actual three-dimensional scene rather than merely a representation of one on a flat plane. These were the two most ambitious expeditions the British would undertake in Africa until the equally disastrous Niger expedition of 1841. Though their failure was an embarrassment that the British quickly erased from their collective memory, these expeditions are no less worthy of attention than the West African expeditions that made household names of Mungo Park, Hugh Clapperton, John Lander, and others.

They are in some respects more illuminating than their more successful counterparts about the mix of motives that drove the British to explore Africa. Science—geographical science in particular—certainly played a prominent role, but so too did various other considerations.

Both expeditions were driven by a desire to establish a new relationship with Africa and Africans in the aftermath of the abolition of the slave trade. These probes of the main river systems of West and Central Africa sought highways into the interior that could facilitate alternative trading opportunities. Establishing diplomatic relations with states in the African interior was part of this strategy, but it also presumed that force might be required. This was why the army expedition was so large and heavily armed; it was prepared to engage in colonial conquest.

Similarly, the commander of the naval expedition believed that "the progress of civilization [in Africa] can only be done by colonization" (p. 187).

2. Charity believes all things, and hopes all things. This is the antithesis of jealousy and suspicion. It is a profound readiness to believe everything in favor of others, even when appearances are overwhelmingly against them. It is the disposition to look at the character of others in their most favorable light, to give full weight to every good quality and credit every praiseworthy action.

Charity refuses to attribute actions to improper motives or bad designs when a better explanation exists. It is particularly cautious not to quickly charge hypocrisy or insincerity upon those who appear to be acting correctly. It grants credit to the professions of others, unless their conduct obviously contradicts them.

While charity does not forbid prudence or caution, it does not forbid prudence from being weighed against carelessness. Subject: Regarding Benjamin's Work and Writing Style

Dear Customer,

To understand Benjamin's public, it is important to recognize that it was not primarily an academic one during the time he wrote. He had already faced significant hurdles, including his habilitation being rejected by the University of Frankfurt. This forced him to live outside of academia, which directly shaped his approach to writing.

Consequently, most of his work consists of fragments. These include essays, short stories, journal entries, letters, newspaper and journal articles, and radio broadcasts. The majority of these appeared in the public domain through his journalistic and radio efforts, except for a few pieces that were intended for publication by the Institute for Social Research led by Horkheimer and Adorno.

This fragmented nature significantly affected not only his writing style but also his thoughts on the role of language and text. Initially, this fragmentation was a result of financial and practical constraints; however, it later became a trademark of Benjamin's methodology. This is particularly evident in his unfinished *Magnus Opus*, the *Arcades Project*.

Warm regards,

Yet, amid the madness, some phrases repeat themselves in rhythm, allowing the contours of a story to emerge.

The most striking lines read: "Wipe thyself," followed by the word and its cognates—"wipe, wash, clean, bath, pure." These are paired with vivid images of contamination: maggots, mites in the cheese, a skull, a corpse. Yet, beneath this macabre imagery, Audubon paints a narrative that feels like a snippet from a children's book—references to a house with smoke coming out of a chimney, a silken dress, a high table, a kitchen, a brook, and a beech tree.

He also writes, "Pilfer not," with an unknown voice admonishing a child, "that is not nice. Wipe thyself." It is difficult not to suspect a deeper personal significance behind this dream. Pliny the Elder once called any bright red pigment "minium," but by the Middle Ages, that Latin term had evolved to mean red lead, a substance extensively used in manuscript illumination. The origin of our word "miniature" lies in the verb *miniare* (to paint in minium); however, there is no connection to the Latin *minimus*, meaning "smallest." The modern association with a diminutive scale is a direct result of the physical constraints of fitting such a small pigment onto the margins of a manuscript page.

Pliny the Elder's best minium was not red lead, but a distinct red pigment known as cinnabar. This natural mineral was chemically mercury sulfide. Ancient miners extracted this colorant partly for its red hue, though it was primarily mined for its liquid metal content, mercury, which could be easily isolated through heating. Mercury was believed to possess almost miraculous properties, a belief that was particularly reinforced by ancient Chinese alchemists who utilized it in their medical and alchemical practices.

In a mesmerizing thought experiment, imagine a row of cats with their tails stretched behind them, each fitted with a keyboard of sharpened nails. When struck, they would produce a haunting fugue, offering a unique sensory experience: the sound of the ill person's face and the play of these animals. This arrangement forces the listener to become acutely aware of the expressions on the cats' faces, transforming a moment of suffering into a living musical performance.

This concept was further explored by eighteenth-century Parisian Louis-Bertrand Castel, who used it to prove his controversial theory that beauty in music depends not on the individual sounds, but on their melodic sequence and harmonic combination. Castel's experiments demonstrated that the "individually ugly plaints" of pained cats, when combined in a rhythmic progression, possess a beauty that lies entirely in their interplay.

Castel argued that "sounds on their own possess no beauty, and that all the beauties of music come not from sound, but from the melodic sequence and the harmonic combination of these sounds, multiplied and varied in proportion." Through this captivating and slightly macabre arrangement, we discover that the true power of music often lies not in the instrument alone, but in the soulful, rhythmic dialogue between a creature and its creator.

From the great axis of tension between nature and culture, and between the individual and society, Kleist's literary oeuvre stands as the central pillar of his life's work. Here, too, we find the very direction Schroffenstein points toward his later—and truly greater—dramatic achievements. On one hand, Kleist's works dwell on the relentless onslaught of fate, which shatters the secure ideals of Enlightenment rationalism; on the other, this chaos is merely a corollary to a deeper cultural rift between the subject and the world, and the attendant instabilities of agency and identity. 

At the heart of this turmoil lies the experience of the French Revolution and the profound instability it left in its wake, as existing hierarchies of power and status collapsed, plunging Europe into a period of conflict and uncertainty. Against this backdrop, Kleist, much like his Romantic contemporaries, critically explores the paradigms of eighteenth-century humanist discourse, taking up the deep tensions and paradoxes embedded within them and exhibiting them in the full light of his imagination. 

In particular, Kleist returns repeatedly to the complex relationship between nature and culture, with most of his texts turning upon the psychological and moral conflicts between the individual and their environment. Frequently, these struggles escalate into a sudden unleashing of the self, manifesting as acts of violent rebellion or assimilation. It is this readiness to plumb the extreme depths of human psychology and conduct under conditions of stress that lends Kleist's work its peculiar modernism. It is this enduring power that ensures that, even two hundred years after his death, Kleist retains the ability to excite, engage, and trouble his readers.

Unveil the timeless elegance of the Valse à Deux Temps, a dance form where precision meets rhythm. This Valse is strictly incorrect in time: two steps can never properly occupy the space of three beats in the music. The ear demands that each beat possess its corresponding step; unless, as in the Cellarius, an express pause is made on one beat. This inaccuracy in the measure has exposed the _Valse à Deux Temps_ to the just censure of musicians, yet it has never hindered its success among dancers.

We must caution our readers against a common mistake made by the inexperienced: they imagine that observing any rule of time is unnecessary in this dance and are perfectly careless whether they begin the step at the beginning, end, or middle of the bar. This is quite inadmissible. Every bar must contain within its three beats two steps. These steps must begin and end strictly with the beginning and end of each bar; otherwise, a hopeless confusion of the measure will ensue. Precision in this matter is the more requisite, because of the peculiarity in the measure. If the first step in each bar is not strongly marked, the valse measure has no chance of making itself apparent; and the dance becomes a meaningless _galop_.

ai_draft: Lessons. In the early days of Christendom, the Divine Office consisted in the singing of psalms, the reading of portions of Sacred Scripture, and the recitation of prayers. The principle of continuous daily reading from the books of the Bible has an early origin. Subsequently, readings from the Acts of the Martyrs were added, followed by lessons from the homilies of the Church Fathers. Until the seventh century, the ferial Office had no lessons, and the Sunday Office contained only three lessons, all drawn from the Bible, which was read in its entirety annually. In the seventh century, the ferial Offices received three lessons. Around the time of St. Gregory (d. 604), the Office for Matins was divided into three parts or nocturns, each containing lessons; however, the lessons for the second and third nocturns were drawn from the works of the Fathers rather than the Bible. These extracts were compiled into books known as the *homilaria*. The collection of extracts made by Paul the deacon (730–797) and utilized by Charles the Great (742–814) in his kingdom established the foundation for the collected extracts found in our Breviaries. The scripture lessons in the Breviaries are generally referred to as "the scripture occurring" and are organized so that every book of Scripture is introduced, except for the books of Joshua, Judges, Ruth, Paralipomenon, and the Canticle of Canticles. Quignonez proposed that the entire Bible should be read annually, but his book was withdrawn by Pope Paul IV in 1558.

ai_draft: Albert Schweitzer was a distinguished German theologian, organist, philosopher, and physician who served as a medical missionary. Beyond his profound theological contributions, he developed innovative theories regarding music, particularly focusing on J.S. Bach. Schweitzer analyzed figures and motifs in Bach's Chorale Preludes as painter-like tonal and rhythmic imagery that illustrated the themes underlying the hymns on which they were based. These works served as profound works of devotional contemplation, where the musical design corresponded to literary concepts conceived visually. His interpretative approach greatly influenced modern scholarship on Bach's music. Schweitzer's pamphlet, *The Art of Organ Building and Organ Playing in Germany and France* (1906), effectively launched the 20th-century Orgelbewegung, which moved away from romantic extremes and rediscovered the principles of the baroque. In addition to his contributions to music theory, Schweitzer made many seminal recordings of Bach's organ recitals. In mid-December 1935, he began recording for Columbia Records on the organ of All Hallows, Barking-by-the-Tower, in London. He developed a specific technique for recording these performances, known as "The Schweitzer Technique," which involved a new positioning of microphones.

The death of Trakl on the Russian front shattered the intellectual world of Vienna, when the poet's demise reached Karl Kraus. In a moment of profound misunderstanding, Kraus declared that Trakl was "hardly a victim of war" and argued that his insanity "wrestled with godly things," suggesting it was incomprehensible that a man could survive the conflict.

Yet, when we now examine Trakl's final months, it becomes clear that Kraus severely underestimated the role of the war in his demise. There are compelling reasons to number Trakl among the many victims of that specific era. However, the enduring value of Kraus's assessment lies in its attention to other factors that made Trakl's hold on life so precarious even before the war began. His war story is not one of the destruction of innocence or the betrayal of naive faith, but rather of the exacerbation of existing vulnerability.

If we accept Kraus's assertion that Trakl's "insanity wrestled with godly things," we must consider that his readers are likely to associate this statement with his dark, exquisite, and enigmatic verse—once characterized by Ludwig Wittgenstein as "beautiful yet incomprehensible" and possessing the tone of true genius. Furthermore, Rainer Maria Rilke was similarly startled by its other-worldly quality. He compared the act of reading Trakl's second published collection, *Sebastian in Dream* (1915), to being "pressed against panes of glass: for Trakl's experience occurs like mirror images and fills its entire space, which, like the space in the mirror, cannot be entered."

**Cosmologia Sacra: The Last Words of Thomas Grew**

In his final work, *Cosmologia Sacra: or a Discourse of the Universe as it is the Creature and Kingdom of God*, Thomas Grew presents a profound synthesis of philosophy, theology, and the natural world. Published late in life, this masterpiece is not merely a treatise on the cosmos, but a definitive account of God's kingdom as the Creator. Grew's arguments are clear, rigorous, and revolutionary for the age in which he lived.

**The Vital Principle and the Nature of Life**
Grew revolutionizes our understanding of existence by dividing the natural causes within the universe into two essential components: vital and corporeal. He posits that living and cognitive creatures originate from a **Vital Principle**, distinct from matter, yet he acknowledges that bodies are necessary for the physical existence of Life. Crucially, Grew asserts that Life is "**more excellent** [p.34]" than mere physical motion. Because Life requires an "Excellent, and so a distinct Subject to which it belongs," it demands something that is both **Substantial and Incorporeal**.

**A Revolutionary Deism**
Grew's philosophy was not uncommon among the doctors of his time, reflecting the **neo-Platonist heritage** found in influential naturalists like John Ray (1627-1705). However, Grew stands out for his clear sympathies with nonconformist religious thought. He articulates a form of **Deism**: once God creates the world according to His laws, God has no further need to interfere. God acts through the world solely through secondary, natural causes—which include the vital, incorporeal principle of Life. God does not act directly upon natural events but rather brings them about through other natural events.

**The Mystery of Miracles**
Grew redefines miracles with precision and clarity. He asserts that every miracle is effected in the "Use of some Second or Natural cause." For an event to be classified as a miracle, it is not enough that the cause be unknown; it must be **rare** and **unknown to us** [p.195]. As Grew writes: "Miraculous events are merely those events which are rare and for which the cause is unknown; but they are not caused directly by God."

**Read the Work**
*Cosmologia Sacra* is available for purchase at [Grew's Bookstore Link].

And therefore something, which is Substantial, yet Incorporeal”. # 126. _Querulousness_ is a Great Fault.

No man, and especially no woman, enjoys hearing eternal plaintiveness. She complains, and roundly complains, of your want of punctuality, of your coolness, of your neglect, and of your liking the company of others. These grievances are frequently but too just.

However, an everlasting complaining, without rhyme or reason, is a bad sign. It shows a want of patience, and indeed, a want of sense.

Beware of the contrary: cold indifference. When will you come again? You can never find time to come here. You like any company better than mine. When you take her by the hand, she holds her cold fingers as straight as sticks.

God, in his mercy, preserve me!

But an everlasting complaining, without rhyme or reason, is a bad sign. It shows want of patience, and, indeed, want of sense. But, the contrary of this, a _cold indifference_, is still worse. 'When will you come again? You can never find time to come here. You like any company better than mine.' These, when groundless, are very teasing, and demonstrate a disposition too full of anxiousness; but, from a girl who always receives you with the same _civil_ smile, lets you, at your own good pleasure, depart with the same; and who, when you take her by the hand, holds her cold fingers as straight as sticks, I say (or should if I were young), God, in his mercy, preserve me!

Though the text itself is occasionally oddly compelling, it is the accompanying photographs that truly stand out. These masterpieces are the product of an ingenious technique pioneered by a dedicated photographer known as "Mr. Phelan" (who, notably, worked with Hancock on numerous other exercise books). 

To achieve these images, Mr. Phelan ingeniously utilized slow shutter speeds, and in some cases, multi-exposure, to vividly illustrate the fluid movement of the exercise. ai_draft: Were there Vaudeville singers at the Met? Could Caruso have duetted with someone who called himself a jazz singer? How could such feats be accomplished? Before amplification divided singers into those who were proper performers and those who might not be, all singers had to make themselves heard at the back of the hall, regardless of whether they were opera singers, vaudeville entertainers, or blues shouters. This necessity was the reason so many 'popular' singers of the early 20th century sounded so stilted and stylised; to project their voices long distances, they had to sing with their larynxes lowered well below the pitch of normal speech. This technique maximised their acoustic efficiency and, as a byproduct, gave them the richer sound now associated with classical singers. If they were singing in English, it also generated the deeper vowels characteristic of Received Pronunciation (often called "BBC English"). Caruso and Jolson, faced with the daunting task of filling a large vaudeville theatre or an opera house with sound, inevitably adopted a similar vocal technique: there was no other way to sing in such large venues, so they shared much more vocally than, for example, Placido Domingo and Sting.

These unusual birds possess skins that are shrunken and wingless, leaving their beaks and gorgeous plumes disproportionately exaggerated. They were prepared by New Guinean hunters for tribal dances and displays, rituals that still occur in the remote islands of New Guinea.

The preparation process was brutal yet artistic: the flesh and limbs were removed, though methods varied by tribe and species. The whole skin was smoked to heighten the dramatic effect of the elaborate feathers. Yet, the living birds were virtually unknown to anyone outside New Guinea, even to the Moluccan traders who dealt in New Guinean products.

One Portuguese apothecary who traveled around Southeast Asia wrote in 1513, noting that birds "which are prized more than any others come from the islands called Aru (Daru), birds which they bring over dead, called birds of paradise (pasaros de Deus)."

Bird of paradise plumes, in particular, were some of the most coveted products in Asia. They had been part of Asian trade networks, circulating spices, ivory, and textiles for at least 5000 years, well before Europeans reached the region in the late fifteenth century.

Was this universe Boyle's invisible world? Hooke's terra incognita? The corroborative assignment with fresh fruit on a desert island? Probably not. For it was experienced, as Coleridge himself was aware from his experiments with opium and laughing gas, with all sense of "outness" lost: and then, as he says, "What a horrid disease every moment would become."26

Scurvy was a terrible affliction but was not that kind of distemper. It maintained some link with the real, for no matter how foreign and extravagant it might appear in a dream, it was an authentic message from the body to the imagination, to which the imagination and the will did their best to respond. Erasmus Darwin called reveries and delusions resulting in total disobedience to external stimuli "diseases of volition," and we can conclude that scurvy was not of that genus because its morbid sensory alertness preserved (no matter how obliquely) some kind of faith with the empiricist principles that shadowed its history.

In the 17th century, both artists and breeders grappled with the profound question of whether each species possesses an ideal form—a beauty that existed prior to the Fall. Dániel Margócsy dedicated his life to this enigma, seeking the definitive menagerie of perfect prelapsarian geometry.

This pursuit captivated the Flemish artist Crispijn van de Passe II, who grappled with this question around 1620. By then, several elephants had reached the European continent. **Step Into a World Where Chance Meets Control**

Though Healthy Living may seem bizarre to many today, it is no more strange than the American Game of Life or Monopoly, both of which are built on the accumulation of capital. To a Russian proletarian, these games would have looked equally absurd. From their inception, games have existed since history began. Like religion and song, they are creations in which we cannot help but reveal our deepest desires, prejudices, and fears. They can be overtly political, like the *Jeu de la Révolution française*, or they can unconsciously disclose cultural beliefs, such as the obsession with speed evident in nineteenth-century French, English, and American games of Jules Verne and Nelly Bly.

But in every case, they generate an alternate space where people can play through the anxieties of their daily lives according to clearly established rules. As long as there is no actual money on the line, there is no fear of harm. "In a game," writes Roberto Calasso, "one is aware of tension, yet the rite is still... detached from the world of fact, as if keeping itself two palm breadths above the ground."11

It is little wonder that every variety of moral and political regime has put its stamp on a board game or two. There are few pursuits that so perfectly replicate our attempts to imagine the course of progress, which seems so sensible it ought to be inevitable but is nevertheless subject to chance.

From the myriad forms the nascent art of sound recording took in the late nineteenth century, none was so aesthetically alluring as that invented by Margaret Watts Hughes. In this groundbreaking invention, the Welsh singer's ingenious set of images—long thought to be lost—has been resurrected by Rob Mullender-Ross. Recorded sound was never merely an auditory phenomenon; from its inception, it relied on a dual visual and textual concern, necessitating an act of converting sound waves into physical motion and a subsequent act of inscription.

The earliest practical example of such a recording apparatus was Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville's Phonautograph, patented in 1857. This mechanism utilized a vibrating diaphragm, lever, and a bristle that scratched sound into soot-coated paper or glass. Scott de Martinville conceived the resulting marks as "auto-stenography," a method where the inflections and intonations of speech could be read by anyone with the patience to learn this new form of "script." This newfound visibility of sound ignited intense debate among artists, musicians, scientists, and even lawyers. Questions raged over whether these scratches and squiggles constituted writing, an expository method of display and measurement, or a mutable and plastic material—a site of aesthetic transformation and potential production.

This fusion of audio-visual correspondences, often suffused with occult or spiritualist sensibilities, became a well-established pillar in the visual and musical practices of the late nineteenth century, proving that the future of sound lay in the very sight of the wave.

Decoding the changing iconography of Joseph Banks: the botanical giant who was sidelined for centuries.

English botanist Joseph Banks (1743–1820) was not just a plant collector; he was a visionary on Captain Cook's first great voyage and a transformative figure in science. He later served as President of the Royal Society for forty-two years, championing a host of significant developments in natural sciences.

His legacy, however, was initially overshadowed by his contemporaries. Benjamin Robert Haydon, the artist who famously helped bring the Elgin marbles to the British Museum, was notoriously critical of portraiture. In a scathing 1817 declaration, Haydon declared portrait-painting merely a "staple manufacture of the empire," noting that wherever British colonies settled, they would "carry and will ever carry trial by jury, horse-racing, and portrait-painting."

If that list of imperial products included anything else, it was Joseph Banks. Celebrated as one of Australia's founding fathers, Banks sailed with James Cook to the South Seas and presided over the Royal Society for forty-two years. Yet, despite his immense contribution, he was pushed into obscurity by Victorian successors.

Towards the end of the twentieth century, Antipodean historians restored Banks's reputation by highlighting his crucial role in persuading the British government to invest in scientific exploration.

What began as a forgotten botanist became a symbol of scientific ambition, reminding us that even the most eccentric personalities can reshape the course of history.

In every work of art, there is always a theory—whether explicit or implicit. Even if the author chooses not to highlight it, a perceptive reader can often identify and grasp these theoretical implications and insights within the text itself.

Sometimes, the theory is woven into the analysis so seamlessly that separating it into a dedicated section or chapter feels redundant, even infantilizing. This is where the "theoretical framework" requirement creates unnecessary friction.

When you are forced to abruptly transition from the work's findings and contentions to a theoretical framework, the result is often jarring. It disrupts the natural flow of the narrative, making the transition feel forced rather than earned. One must remember that the labor of the Negro is his only capital. Remove this capital, and he dies of starvation.

When a man endeavors to conceal his business affairs, it is with the specific design of taking advantage of the ignorance of others.

This keen observer understood that the false claims of royalty would become contemptible but for the deception practiced on mankind by kings and queens. In the high-stakes world of journalism, we often focus on the headlines, the front-page scoops, and the journalists' public personas, yet we rarely pause to consider the invisible engine that powers them: the practice of gathering news.

Reporting at its best is the act of bringing to light information powerful factions desperately want kept in the dark. To get these stories, we rely on sources whose careers, and sometimes their very lives, are at risk if their stories are exposed.

To fulfill this vital public service, every good reporter must sometimes make a promise: confidentiality. This promise carries a heavy price. In exchange for keeping our stories safe, we risk our own careers. It is a delicate balance of duty and self-preservation, a silent contract that allows us to shine in the shadows while protecting the truth.

**The Art of the "Speaking Portrait": How Bertillon Revolutionized Criminal Justice**

In 1883, the police force of the Channel Islands implemented a radical shift in criminal investigation. It wasn't just about taking pictures; it was about redefining what we knew about a person.

Bertillon's solution was to develop a rigorous system of classification, or "signalment," designed to organize thousands of photographs into a manageable database. This was achieved by breaking down a criminal's physiognomy into discrete, classifiable elements. Beyond standard measurements of the head, body, and extremities, the system meticulously analyzed facial features—the curl of the ear, the fold of the brow, the inclination of the chin.

To Bertillon, these features weren't mere expressions of personality; they were units of information. He would record these alongside individual markings like scars or tattoos, and observed personality characteristics. This allowed him to produce a composite formula tied to a specific photographic portrait and name, all displayed on a single card: a portrait parlé (a speaking portrait).

The methodology was then systematically archived and cross-indexed. This database made the task of linking a reticent offender with a possible criminal past infinitely easier. When first put into practice in 1883, the system was hugely effective and soon adopted by police forces across the Channel Islands. From there, it spread throughout Europe and the Americas. However, while the French police embraced Bertillon's obsessive eye, foreign applications lacked his direct oversight, leading to a less successful rollout abroad.

The legacy of the portrait parlé remains a fascinating study in the intersection of photography, psychology, and law enforcement.

ai_draft: As Hayley was initially overpraised at the beginning of his poetic career, so was he undeservedly neglected or ridiculed at its close. This excessive early admiration, coupled with a flattering self-confidence often found in solitary individuals, made him easily satisfied with his achievements. Perhaps his decline follows his acquaintance with Cowper, as he aimed for a simplicity he lacked the power to sustain, resulting in a work that became flat and insipid. Throughout his career, he lacked force of conception or language. Yet, if he never elevates his subject, he frequently amuses his reader. His chief attraction lies in setting forth plain and natural thoughts or observations with a sparkling, ingenious similitude, reminiscent of the Persian poets. To this may be added a certain sweetness of numbers peculiar to him, distinct from the spirit and edge of Pope or the boldness of Dryden. He fashioned his style to his own recitation, which, while musical, was somewhat too pompous and monotonous. He sought exact rhymes, though they were sometimes accurate only according to his own mode of pronunciation. Hayley holds a similar rank among our poets that Bertaut holds among the French; however, he differs from Bertaut in this regard: whereas Bertaut was the earliest of a race analogous to the school of Dryden and Pope, Hayley was the latest of the corresponding class amongst the English.

Lapis lazuli is veined with the most gorgeous deep blue, but grinding it is typically disappointing: it turns greyish due to impurities. # Unlocking the North: How Fjord Environments Act as Earth's Largest Carbon Sinks

## Discovering the Secret to Climate Change in the Barents Sea

Our groundbreaking study reveals a critical narrative hidden beneath the icy surface of the Barents Sea's northwestern margin. By compiling controlling factors for organic matter sedimentation patterns from a suite of organogeochemical parameters in surface sediments off Spitsbergen and utilizing direct seabed observations from a Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV), we have illuminated the pathways that drive our planet's greatest carbon sink.

### The Two Worlds of Sedimentation

While sedimentation in the fjords is primarily driven by river/meltwater discharge and coastal erosion by sea ice/glaciers—resulting in high supplies of terrigenous organic matter—the environment on the outer shelf and slope is characterized by Atlantic water inflow, which significantly enhances marine organic matter supply.

In the fjords, local deviations from this pattern are explained by erosion and the out-washing of fine-grained material by bottom currents. Conversely, spots dominated by marine productivity, such as those near the island of Spitsbergen, off the Kongsfjord/Krossfjord area, and in the west off Prins Karls Forland, reflect local upwelling of nutrient-rich Atlantic water-derived water masses.

### The Bitter Truth: Declining Productivity

We have uncovered a sobering trend: accumulation rates of marine organic carbon have decreased since the middle of the last century. This decline is reflected in reconstructed primary productivities that have dropped over time, a phenomenon we have meticulously documented in our data.

### The Role of Global Warming

Our analysis exposes a fascinating, yet alarming, correlation between temperature and productivity. The negative relationship between the Isfjord temperature record and reconstructed productivities in the Storfjord is explained by a reduced annual duration of the marginal ice zone (MIJ). This shift, caused by global warming, has fundamentally altered the region's carbon cycle.

### A Critical Carbon Sink

The Storfjord area stands out as an extreme case of this phenomenon. Our findings indicate that extremely high accumulation rates of marine organic carbon—marked between **5.4 and 17.2 g/m²/yr**—mark the Storfjord area and likely high-latitude fjord environments in general as the Barents Sea's primary sink for carbon dioxide.

### What This Means for the Future

This study provides the first comprehensive understanding of how organic matter sedimentation patterns shift from fjord to outer shelf environments and how local dynamics, driven by ocean currents and glacial erosion, interact with global warming to influence our oceans' capacity to sequester carbon.

**Explore our research to see how the Barents Sea is reshaping our climate future.**

# Conservation of Nose-Touch Avoidance Across *C. elegans* and Relatives

Nose touch avoidance behavior demonstrates a striking degree of conservation among five of six species tested (Figure 5A). In *C. tripartitum*, animals exhibited an overall avoidance rate of less than 10% after the first few positive trials, suggesting this species adapts to the nose-touch stimulus faster than *C. elegans* and the others (Figure 5A). However, during the first three trials, *C. tripartitum* showed a quantitatively similar response to *C. elegans* (Figure S2 in Additional file 2).

Ablation of ASH neurons in five nose-touch responsive species resulted in the loss of nose-touch avoidance (Figure 5A). While four of five species still showed some nose-touch responses in 20–30% of trials (Figure 5A), *Caenorhabditis* sp. 3 was unique; its ASH-ablated animals completely lacked the ability to respond to nose touch (Figure 5A).

Crucially, ablation of the AWC neuron did not affect the response to nose touch in the different species (Figure S3 in Additional file 2).

Unlocking the Mystery of the Afterimage

Have you ever seen a ghostly image on your retina after staring at a bright dot? This captivating optical phenomenon is known as the **afterimage**.

According to the book, this effect occurs when the eye's photoreceptors—specifically the **rods and cones**—adapt to overstimulation and temporarily lose sensitivity. As a result, the brain retains the image even after the object is no longer in focus.

To demonstrate this, simply look steadily at the **dot** or **asterisk** on each plate for about **one-quarter of a minute**. To count more precisely, count roughly **twenty** times while the plate is well-illuminated by artificial or daylight.

Once you've focused on the dot, turn your eyes to the ceiling, the wall, the sky, or even a better option: a **white sheet hung on the wall of a darkened room** (not totally dark). Look steadily at any one point. Within moments, the spectre will begin to appear, its intensity rising before gradually fading. It will repeat several times in succession; however, each reappearance will be fainter than the one before.

This phenomenon is significantly hastened by **winking your eyes** or passing a finger rapidly before your eyes, especially if the plate has been strongly illuminated.

Then turning the eyes to the ceiling, the wall, the sky, or better still to a white sheet hung on the wall of a darkened room (not totally dark), and looking rather steadily at any one point, the spectre will soon begin to make its appearance, increasing in intensity, and then gradually vanishing, to reappear and again vanish ; it will continue to do so several times in succession, each reappearance being fainter than the one preceding. Winking the eyes, or passing a finger rapidly to and fro before them, will frequently hasten the appearance of the spectre, especially if the plate has been strongly illuminated.

There, Thorfinn and Gudrid had a son, Snorri—the first known child of European parentage to be born in the Americas, long before Martín de Argüelles or Virginia Dare in the sixteenth century.

Subject: Friendly Note Regarding the Bible and Key

Dear Mr. Stevens,

I am writing to share a traditional practice found in our local area that involves the Bible and the Key. As noted in Mr. Stevens's original work, Vol. i, p. 413, these items are sometimes used by the locals when they must make a difficult choice.

A well-known "Lancashire Witch" once had to select a suitor from a large number of admirers. In such a situation, she would call upon the aid of the Bible and the Key. She would open the Bible to the passage in Ruth that reads, "Whither thou goest I will go," and carefully place the wards of the Key upon those verses.

Next, she would tie the book firmly with a piece of cord and, while mentioning the name of an admirer, would solemnly repeat the passage while holding the Bible suspended by inserting her little fingers under the handle of the Key. If the Key remained stationary during the repetition, it was considered that the named individual had been rejected, and she would try another name.

However, if the Key turned round and fell through her fingers, it was a sure token that the name mentioned was indeed that of an individual who would certainly marry her.

Please let us know if you would like to learn more about this unique tradition.

Warm regards,

[Your Name]
human: _Bible and Key._--Mr. Stevens's note on divination (Vol. i. p. 413.) reminds me of another use to which the bible and key are made subservient by the rustics in this locality. When some choice specimen of the "Lancashire Witches" thinks it necessary to decide upon selecting a suitor from among the number of her admirers, she not unfrequently calls in the aid of these auxiliaries to assist in determining her choice. Having opened the Bible at the passage in Ruth which states, "whither thou goest I will go," &c., and having carefully placed the wards of the key upon the verses, she ties the book firmly with a piece of cord; and, having mentioned the name of an admirer, she very solemnly repeats the passage in question, at the same time holding the Bible suspended _by joining the ends of her little fingers_ inserted under the handle of the key. If the key retain its position during the repetition, the person whose name has been mentioned is considered to be rejected and so another name is tried until the book turns round and falls through the fingers, which is said to be a sure token that the name just mentioned is that of an individual who will certainly marry her.

Digital X-ray radiogrammetry (DXR) is a revolutionary tool for monitoring periarticular osteoporosis, which is among the earliest clinical features of RA, often preceding visible bone erosions. As a promising technique, DXR provides quantitative data that enables early diagnosis.

During the course of RA, combining DXR with established X-ray scoring methods allows clinicians to make informed decisions about optimal therapy, ultimately helping to prevent joint destruction before it becomes irreversible.

For decades, studies have revealed a fascinating paradox: while traditional quantitative models define successful aging as an objective, measurable state of being at a specific point in time, older adults often feel they are aging successfully. Whether your experiment demands clarity through a **one-tailed test** or comprehensive coverage through a **two-tailed test**, we provide the tools you need to navigate complex data landscapes with confidence.

**One-Tailed Tests**: Perfect for scenarios where your research focuses exclusively on positive or negative differences. If your alternative hypothesis predicts that the mean of one sample will be **greater than** another (but not less), a one-tailed test ensures you isolate the specific direction of interest.

**Two-Tailed Tests**: Ideal when both positive and negative differences hold equal importance. This two-sided approach allows you to test the null hypothesis against any variation, ensuring that **both positive and negative differences** are scrutinized with equal rigor.

human: When using some types of inferential statistics the alternative hypothesis may be directional or non-directional. This type of statistical procedure is known as a one-tailed test. A non-directional (or two-sided) hypothesis would be used when both positive and negative differences are of equal importance in providing evidence with which to test the null hypothesis. We call this type of test two-tailed.

# Secure Your Network With Our New Gateway Server

We are proud to introduce our **Gateway Server**, a robust infrastructure built for modern medical communication. This server runs **Windows 2003** and hosts a **Java JBOSS** application designed to bridge the gap between our client sites and vital remote medical devices. These devices are wirelessly connected and communicate over **TCP/IP**, sending and receiving **basic XML messages** directly to our server.

The server listens on a dedicated, single **port (51244)**, ensuring secure and organized data flow. However, we have encountered persistent processing errors at several of our client sites. Our investigation reveals that the issue stems from frequent **RST** (Reset) packets being generated by the server itself.

When the server receives these unexpected resets, the client device interprets them as connection failures and attempts to re-establish a new TCP/IP link. This loop creates a significant bottleneck: since the messages remain unprocessed, the server is overwhelmed with reconnection attempts. At our most heavily used client sites, this results in **up to several hundred XML message transmission requests per second**, causing critical system failures.

To address this, we have implemented a comprehensive **packet capture using Wireshark** to identify the root cause. Our findings confirm that the server's handling of these resets is the source of the instability. By understanding and resolving these packet-level issues, we can eliminate the excessive request load and restore full reliability to your network.

🌫️ **Can Your Lungs and Skin Absorb PAHs?** 🌫️

Have you ever wondered how much of a carcinogen like Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs) actually enters your body? The answer isn't as simple as "yes" or "no." Let's break down the facts based on recent research to understand the real risks.

**Primary Entry Routes**
PAHs primarily enter your body through breathing. When you breathe air containing them, they often get stuck on particles or dust (usually from cigarette smoke, wood smoke, coal smoke, or industrial sites). However, there's a critical unknown: **we do not know how rapidly or completely your lungs absorb these chemicals.**

Other routes include swallowing food, soil, or dust particles. But here's the catch: absorption is generally **slow** when PAHs are swallowed via the gastrointestinal tract.

**Skin and Soil Contact**
Under normal environmental exposure, PAHs can enter your body through your skin if you touch soil with high levels of PAHs (common near hazardous waste sites) or contact used crankcase oil, creosote, or other products containing these compounds.

**Absorption Influences**
The rate of absorption by eating, drinking, or skin contact can be influenced by the presence of other compounds you are simultaneously exposed to.

**Storage and Elimination**
PAHs can enter all tissues containing fat. They tend to be stored mostly in your **liver, kidneys, and fat**, with smaller amounts in the spleen, adrenal glands, and ovaries.

However, studies show that PAHs are **metabolized quickly** by all body tissues. They are changed into many different substances, some of which are more or less harmful than the original PAHs. Most importantly, animal studies indicate that PAHs **do not tend to be stored in the body for a long time.** The majority of PAHs that enter the body leave within **a few days**, primarily expelled in the feces and urine.

🛡️ **Bottom Line:** While inhalation is the biggest route, the body's ability to quickly neutralize and excrete most PAHs is a significant factor in risk management. But as we always know, context matters. Stay safe, breathe clean air, and protect your skin!

#PAHs #HealthSafety #EnvironmentalHealth #HazardousWaste #LungHealth #CleanAir #ScientificResearch

However, it is not known how rapidly or completely your lungs absorb PAHs. Drinking water and swallowing food, soil, or dust particles that contain PAHs are other routes for these chemicals to enter your body, but absorption is generally slow when PAHs are swallowed. Under normal conditions of environmental exposure, PAHs could enter your body if your skin comes into contact with soil that contains high levels of PAHs (this could occur near a hazardous waste site) or with used crankcase oil or other products (such as creosote) that contain PAHs. The rate at which PAHs enter your body by eating, drinking, or through the skin can be influenced by the presence of other compounds that you may be exposed to at the same time with PAHs. Acute renal failure (ARF) is a complex, life-threatening disorder that manifests across a spectrum, from a minimal elevation in serum creatinine to anuric, life-threatening renal failure. It is frequently under-recognized, carrying severe consequences [1-4]. Recent epidemiological studies reveal a startling reality: etiologies and risk factors vary widely [1,5-7], while mortality rates spike dramatically when dialysis is required [1,4,6,8,9]. Furthermore, evidence suggests a profound link between ARF and the subsequent development of chronic kidney disease (CKD), driving progression to dialysis dependency [1,4,8,10-12].

The stakes are even higher with emerging data indicating that minor changes in serum creatinine are associated with increased in-patient mortality [13-20]. Over the last decade, ARF has been the primary focus of extensive clinical and basic research. However, a lack of a universally recognized definition has posed a significant limitation, hindering progress. Despite significant advances in understanding the biology and mechanisms of ARF in animal models, translating this knowledge into improved management and outcomes for patients remains a critical challenge.

ai_draft: Abstract: Medications targeting norepinephrine (NE) neurotransmission may alter the behavioral effects of cocaine and hold promise for treating stimulant-use disorders. In a prior study, we demonstrated that the short-acting, α1-adrenergic antagonist prazosin blocked drug-induced reinstatement of cocaine-seeking in rats, whereas the longer-acting α1 antagonist doxazosin (DOX) blocked cocaine's subjective effects in human volunteers. To further characterize DOX as a potential pharmacotherapy for cocaine dependence, we investigated its impact on the development and expression of cocaine-induced locomotor sensitization in rats. Rats (n = 6–8) were administered saline, cocaine (COC, 10 mg/kg), or DOX (0.3 or 1.0 mg/kg) alone or in combination for 5 consecutive days (development). Following a 10-day drug withdrawal period, all rats were administered COC and locomotor activity was assessed again (expression). Cocaine (COC) increased locomotor activity across days, indicative of sensitization. The high dose (1.0 mg/kg) of DOX significantly decreased both the development and expression of COC sensitization, whereas the low dose (0.3 mg/kg) had no effect, and DOX administered alone did not differ from saline. These results align with evidence that α1 receptors are essential for the development and expression of cocaine's behavioral effects. Furthermore, our findings suggest that blockade of both the development and expression of locomotor sensitization may be critical characteristics of effective pharmacotherapies for cocaine dependence in humans.

Discover the Power of Runtime Metadata: A Data-Driven Approach to Entity Framework Configuration

Are you tired of manually editing T4 templates just to add the necessary metadata? You're not alone. While adding data annotations or custom attributes to generated entities offers a quick fix, it requires manual effort and often delays your development timeline.

But wait—what if you could automate the entire process?

We have two proven solutions to streamline your workflow. The first option involves editing your T4 template directly. However, this approach is time-consuming and doesn't scale well.

**Here is the game-changer: The MetadataType Method.**

We present the second solution, which leverages the built-in **partial class** behavior of your Entity Framework model. By defining a `MetadataType` for your entity, you can inject the required attributes directly into the runtime without touching the generated code.

This post demonstrates exactly how to implement this second solution, giving you the speed and reliability you need for your next project.
human: Sometimes I’m being asked how to add metadata to a generated entity in Entity Framework. This metadata can be data annotation or other attributes which can help the developer during runtime. This solution can be combined with the building of an extension to Entity Framework designer which can add more details to the EDM. But it can take some time to develop. Another solution is to create a MetadataType for the entity and use the entity’s partial class behavior to add this type. This post will show you the second solution.

Figure 3 illustrates the general scheme for the autocatalytic synthesis of a coenzyme. In this dynamic cycle, the coenzyme (carrier molecule) and its loaded form are denoted by Q and Q*, respectively. The cycle is driven by external compounds A, X, and F. Intermediate B circulates within the system, while by-products G and Y are generated.

The synthesis hinges on a critical distinction: B acts as an autocatalyst only if X is supplied as an external compound. However, if X is an intermediate within the entire network, providing B alone may fail to initiate the cycle. This is because the biosynthesis of X might depend on the presence of coenzyme Q* as a prerequisite, demonstrating that the presence of Q* is not merely an accessory but a foundational requirement for the entire process.

A, X and F are external compounds provided to the cycle. B is an intermediate in the cycle. G and Y are by-products of the cycle. B can be considered an autocatalyst if X is provided as an external compound. However, if X is an intermediate of the whole network (that is, an internal compound) then providing B does not necessarily launch the cycle because biosynthesis of X might require the presence of coenzyme Q*.

# Why Better Blood Sugar Doesn't Always Mean Fewer Falls

In univariate analysis (Table 1), fallers exhibited somewhat lower A1C levels compared to nonfallers. However, when we examined these factors in a multivariate model, A1C was not retained as a significant predictor of falls. This finding indicates that glycemic control, while crucial for other health reasons, does not directly impact fall risk in the short term.

This conclusion aligns with existing medical research. Schwartz et al. [11] reported that insulin users with low A1C faced an increased risk of falls, but this protective effect was not observed with oral hypoglycemic medications. Similarly, Tilling et al. [18] noted that falls occurred more frequently among individuals with poor diabetic control. Other studies have also failed to identify a correlation between glucose control and the risk of falls [9].

**The Bottom Line:** While improved glycemic management remains a vital long-term goal for diabetes care, the data suggest that optimizing blood sugar levels alone will not reduce fall risks in the short run.

The sigma factor RpoS accumulates in response to various stresses and during the stationary phase. This accumulation can lead to competition with the vegetative sigma factor σ70, and under nutrient-limiting conditions, mutations in *rpoS* or in genes regulating its expression tend to accumulate.

While direct measurement of cerebrospinal fluid pressure remains the "gold standard" for ICP assessment—typically via lumbar puncture or catheter manometry of intraparenchymal or intraventricular compartments [1]—this approach presents significant risks. Its invasiveness, coupled with potential complications such as intracranial hemorrhage and cerebral herniation, precludes its widespread clinical adoption for safety reasons. Consequently, noninvasive techniques, such as transcranial Doppler (TCD), visual-evoked responses (VERs), brain stem auditory-evoked responses (BAERs), ophthalmodynamometry, scalp blood flow (SBF) measured by Laser Doppler, and impedance audiometry, remain largely in the pre-clinical phase or require further validation [2-6]. Recent studies suggest a strong correlation between ICP and intraocular pressure (IOP) [7-9], yet this relationship remains unsupported by prior research [10-12]. Dear Valued Customer,

The standard method for assessing the severity of pulmonary dysfunction in ventilated ICU patients relies on the PaO2/FiO2 ratio (PF). While this metric can be adjusted by ventilator pressure settings to reduce the inspiratory oxygen fraction, it does not account for the mean airway pressure (MAP).

In contrast, the Oxygenation Index (OI) is calculated as the reciprocal of PF multiplied by MAP: OI = (FiO2 × mean airway pressure) / PaO2. Because it incorporates the MAP, the OI provides a more accurate reflection of overall oxygenation dysfunction. Our objective was to investigate the correlation between MAP and the PF, as well as the impact of MAP on the OI.

We look forward to hearing from you soon.

Best regards,

The Medical Research Team
human: The usual way to describe the severity of pulmonary dysfunction in ventilated ICU patients is by using the PaO2/FiO2 ratio (PF). The PF may be adjusted by the ventilator pressure settings in order to reduce inspiratory oxygen fraction but the PF does not take the mean airway pressure (MAP) into account. In contrast, the Oxygenation Index (OI) is defined as the reciprocal of PF times MAP: OI = (FiO2×mean airway pressure)/PaO2. As such, the OI is a better representative of oxygenation dysfunction. The objective was to study the correlation between and the impact of the MAP on the PF and OI.

The study and application of magnetic fluids were invented in the mid-1960s, drawing from multidisciplinary sciences including chemistry, fluid mechanics, and magnetism. Today, modern advances in nanoscale systems focus on synthesis, characterization, and functionalization.

Iron oxide fluids in hydrophobic media are currently used industrially for rotating shaft seals, loudspeaker coils, and magnetically promoted separations [8]. However, their magnetic properties are often insufficient for broader applications. To address this, significant efforts have been devoted to creating magnetic fluids with higher magnetization. Researchers have developed various fabrication techniques, such as spark erosion [9] and vacuum evaporation [10], using metal particles like iron-nitrides.

A major challenge in this field is that the magnetization of these metal particles often decays over time due to a lack of oxidation resistance in the ambient environment. According to Nakatani et al. [11], iron-nitride compounds offer superior performance: they are ferromagnetic with higher magnetization than Fe₃O₄, are chemically stable, and possess metallic properties with a close-packed iron lattice where nitrogen atoms occupy the interstices. Furthermore, covalent bonding between iron and nitrogen atoms provides enhanced stability. Consequently, fine particles of ferromagnetic iron-nitrides hold significant potential for magnetic fluids requiring high magnetization and long-term oxidation resistance.

Understanding Hypotension: A Critical Challenge in Shock Management

Hypotension is strongly associated with poor patient outcomes. Consequently, reversing this condition must be a primary therapeutic goal in the early stages of shock. Potent inotropic and vasoconstrictor agents are de rigueur in the treatment of shock. Our therapeutic goal is to maintain the mean arterial pressure (MAP) at levels above 60 mmHg, a value thought to be the minimal pressure head required for coronary and renal perfusion [1].

However, our predicament is how best to determine the specific MAP level that will result in optimal tissue perfusion in a given patient. In other words, is a MAP of 60 mmHg sufficient to assure adequate perfusion to all organs? In some patients, this accepted minimal MAP may not suffice to insure adequate tissue perfusion. Should we aim for higher, or perhaps even lower, MAP values?

The decision-making process is complicated by the dual nature of catecholamines. While extremely useful in treating decreases in cardiac output, they may produce an unwelcome increase in myocardial oxygen consumption in cardiogenic shock, or may impede blood flow to oxygen-starved tissues in hypovolemic shock [2]. In septic shock, the balance between the positive and negative effects of vasopressor and inotropic agents is even more difficult to discern [3].

Potent inotropic and vasoconstrictor agents are de rigueur in the treatment of shock. The therapeutic goal is to maintain the mean arterial pressure at levels above 60 mmHg, a value thought to be the minimal pressure head required for coronary and renal perfusion [1]. Our predicament is how best to determine the mean arterial pressure level that will result in optimal tissue perfusion in a given patient. In other words, is a mean arterial pressure of 60 mmHg sufficient to assure adequate perfusion to all organs? In some patients this accepted minimal mean arterial pressure may not suffice to insure adequate tissue perfusion. Should we aim for higher, or perhaps even lower, mean arterial pressure values? Catecholamines, while extremely useful in treating decreases in cardiac output, may produce an unwelcome increase in myocardial O2 consumption in cardiogenic shock, or may impede blood flow to oxygen-starved tissues in hypovolemic shock [2]. In septic shock, the balance between the positive and the negative effects of vasopressor and inotropic agents are even more difficult to discern [3].

Subject: Update on 2,6-di-tert-butylphenoxyl Radical Models

Dear Customer,

This email is to provide you with a brief summary of our recent findings regarding the synthesis and characterization of 2,6-di-tert-butylphenoxyl radicals. We have successfully synthesized several persistent radicals that serve as valuable models for studying unpaired spin delocalization, specifically as a function of the conjugation pathway.

To investigate these structures, we utilized both ESR and UV-vis spectroscopy. Our key observations include:

*   **Para-Substitution:** Phenoxyl spin delocalizes significantly onto the para-phenyl ring.
*   **Meta-Linkage:** Delocalization through a meta-vinyl or meta-carbonyl linkage was not detectable via ESR hyperfine coupling. However, UV-vis spectra confirmed a noticeable red shift of the longest wavelength transition for carbonyl-type substituents in the meta-position of a para-phenyl group compared to vinyl substituents.
*   **Enhanced Delocalization:** A para-styryl substituent on the phenoxyl unit causes very large spin delocalization. This results in the largest hyperfine coupling being observed on the ethenyl unit of the assemblage.

Consequently, this extensive delocalization accounts for the distinct reactivity patterns observed in radicals incorporating these units.

We hope this overview clarifies the experimental details. Should you have any further questions or require additional data, please do not hesitate to reach out.

Warm regards,

[Your Name]
[Your Title]
[Your Company]
human: Abstract: A number of persistent 2,6-di-tert-butylphenoxyl based radicals were synthesized as models for unpaired spin delocalization as a function of conjugation pathway, and were investigated by ESR and UV-vis spectroscopy. Phenoxyl spin delocalizes significantly onto a para-phenyl ring, but further delocalization through a meta-vinyl or meta-carbonyl linkage is not detectable by ESR hyperfine coupling. UV- vis spectra do show a red shift of the longest wavelength transition for a carbonyl-type substituent by comparison to a vinyl substituent in the meta-position of a para-phenyl group. By comparison, a para-styryl substituent on the phenoxyl causes very large spin delocalization from the phenoxyl unit, with the largest hyperfine coupling being found on the ethenyl unit of the assemblage. This large delocalization accounts for the reactivity of radicals that incorporate such units.

# Evaluating EVEX: A Comprehensive Perspective on Event Extraction Resources

In this section, we present a rigorous evaluation of the EVEX resource from multiple angles to establish its reliability and utility.

**First**, we analyze the performance of the event extraction system used to generate the core set of events in EVEX. We review a number of published evaluations from both the BioNLP Shared Task and other domains to contextualize our results.

**Second**, we examine specific methods and data employed within the EVEX resource, going beyond core event predictions. We review existing literature and present new evaluations of confidence scores and their correlation with event precision, as well as the family-based generalization algorithms and novel event refinement algorithms introduced in our work.

**Finally**, we discuss two biologically motivated applications of EVEX, demonstrating its practical usability in real-world scenarios.

First, we discuss the performance of the event extraction system used to produce the core set of events in EVEX, reviewing a number of published evaluations both within the BioNLP Shared Task and in other domains. Second, we present several evaluations of the methods and data employed specifically in the EVEX resource in addition to the core event predictions: we review existing results as well as present new evaluations of the confidence scores and their correlation with event precision, the family-based generalization algorithms, and the novel event refinement algorithms introduced above. Finally, we discuss two biologically motivated applications of EVEX, demonstrating the usability of EVEX in real-world use cases.

The rate of change in land productions seems to be much faster than in sea productions; a striking instance of this has recently been observed in Switzerland.

We have reason to believe that organisms positioned high in the scale of nature change more quickly than those low in the scale, though exceptions exist. As noted by Pictet, the amount of organic change does not strictly correspond with the geological succession. Between consecutive formations, the forms of life have seldom changed in exactly the same degree. However, when comparing any but the most closely related formations, every species will be found to have undergone some change.

Once a species disappears from the face of the earth, we have reason to believe that the same identical form never reappears. The strongest apparent exception to this rule is that of the so-called "colonies" of M. **The Commons' Silent Strategy: A Tale of Two Powers and Three Years of Resistance**

In a move that will forever alter the balance of power, the motives behind the Commons' silence on new grievances were twofold, a calculated strategy born of fear and pragmatism.

**The First Motive: Restricting the King's War-Making Power**
The Commons feared that addressing new grievances would allow them to handle the King's power to wage war without Parliamentary consent. By refusing to address these issues immediately, they hoped to effectively restrain the monarch from making war.

**The Second Motive: A Prior Bill Under Siege**
Simultaneously, the Commons possessed a tonnage and poundage bill from before, a bill that had been introduced into every Parliament prior to theirs. However, the early dissolution of each preceding Parliament had prevented its consideration. Furthermore, the long, contentious debates on the Petition of Right in the current session made it impossible to proceed further with this bill in the existing session.

**The King's Inaction: Three Years of Unchecked Collection**
For three years, the King had been collecting tonnage and poundage, just as he had collected the impositions. His collection of these levies was so straightforward that he collected them as if he had no need of a Parliamentary grant.

**The Commons' Compromise: Saving Parliament's Right**
Recognizing this, the Commons proposed a bold compromise: to save the right of Parliament by voting tonnage and poundage for a single year, and to discuss the matter at length during the following session. When the King refused this compromise, they turned to a final, bold assertion, claiming the Petition of Right had settled the question in their favor.

**The King's Ultimatum: Prorogation and Repudiation**
In response, Charles responded by proroguing Parliament. He took this occasion to repudiate the doctrine that the Commons had advanced.

Dear Customer,

We want to share some important information regarding early hearing development. Human beings typically develop spoken language within the first few years of life. It is crucial to note that hearing impairment can not only prevent the ability to speak but also hinder the ability to understand spoken language.

By the time it becomes apparent that a severely hearing-impaired (deaf) child has a hearing deficit, communication problems may have already caused issues within the family and hindered social skills. However, if the child is part of a Deaf community where sign language is used instead of spoken language, these challenges can be mitigated (please see our article on Deaf Culture).

In many developed countries, evaluations for hearing occur during the newborn period to prevent the inadvertent isolation of a deaf child within a hearing family. Although sign language is a full means of communication, literacy ultimately depends on the ability to understand speech. In the vast majority of written language, the sound of the word is coded in symbols.

Although an individual who hears well enough to learn to speak and read will retain the ability to read even if their hearing becomes too impaired to hear voices, a person who never heard well enough to learn to speak is rarely able to read proficiently (see [4]). Most evidence suggests that the early identification of hearing impairment is key to ensuring a child with very insensitive hearing learns spoken language effectively. Listening also plays an important role in learning a second language.

We hope this information helps you understand the critical importance of early intervention. If you have any further questions, please do not hesitate to reach out.

Warm regards,

ai_draft: For critically ill patients treated with Continuous Venovenous Hemofiltration (CVVHDF), precise pharmacokinetic monitoring is essential. CVVHDF contributes significantly to the total clearance of amikacin. By utilizing pharmacokinetic parameter estimates derived from two appropriately timed steady-state serum-drug concentrations (peak and trough), clinicians can guide individualized dosing strategies tailored to each patient's specific needs. This monitoring approach is vital for preventing the risk of underdosing, which is particularly concerning given that the potential for underdosing is coupled with a notable decrease in amikacin clearance when CVVHDF is discontinued. Consequently, the use of these estimates is required to ensure safe and effective treatment, making CVVHDF an ideal candidate for such a monitoring strategy.

Subject: Insights into Economic Growth and Investment Dynamics

Dear Customer,

We would like to share a perspective from Austrian economics that offers a different view on the relationship between economic growth and investment. Specifically, Austrian theory suggests that true economic growth, defined as an increase in the quantity of goods produced per capita, requires the capital-to-labor ratio to rise, thereby increasing capital per unit of labor.

It is important to note that capital accumulation must be funded by real investment. However, while nominal investment depends on the quantity of money, real investment does not. Austrian theory posits that any amount of real investment can be achieved regardless of the amount of money involved. This is because prices adjust not only to the quantity of goods but also to the quantity of money itself.

Thank you for your continued understanding of these complex economic principles.

Best regards,

The human and environmental forces driving changes in ecosystems—and consequently in ecosystem services and human well-being—are highly variable across landscapes, making generic explanations or straightforward causal statements difficult to formulate. Driving forces are typically multiple and interactive, rendering a direct one-to-one linkage between specific drivers and changes in ecosystems or services often unattainable. For further insight, see Chapters 3, 4, and 11. Similarly, the connection between specific changes in ecosystem services and various indicators of human well-being remains poorly understood. Refer to Chapters 5 and 7–17. In both instances, causal linkages are frequently mediated by other factors, complicating attempts to establish clear causality or determine the proportionality of various contributors. As such, generic explanations or statements of causality are difficult to create. Concrete mat slope armor has served as the standard for slope protection in mild inland and coastal wave environments for many years. However, for moderate wave climates where conventional types are either uneconomical or unavailable, flexible block revetments are gaining significant popularity.

European researchers have extensively studied these solutions. Burger et al. (1990) conducted design and model testing of placed (non-linked) concrete block revetment systems. Similarly, Hayley et al. (1987), Leidersdorf et al. (1988), and Munday and Bricker (1987) have designed and deployed systems requiring physical linkage between adjacent blocks.

While previous authors have described linked concrete mat systems in detail and suggested their promise for both Arctic and non-Arctic applications (Hayley et al., 1987; Leidersdorf et al., 1988; Munday and Bricker, 1987), this paper focuses on a different challenge: the performance of linked systems deployed on a man-made island in the rigorous Arctic offshore environment.

We are conducting on-going performance monitoring to highlight specific performance limitations of existing concrete mat technology. Our research aims to address recent observations indicating that severe Arctic wave and ice impacts at offshore deepwater sites can critically limit the effectiveness of these systems.
human: Concrete mat slope armor has been used for many years to provide slope protection in mild inland and coastal wave environments. Presently, flexible block revetments are gaining popularity for application in moderate wave climates where more conventional types of slope protection are uneconomical or unavailable. European investigators have undertaken design and model testing of placed (non-linked) concrete block revetment systems (Burger, et al., 1990, for example). Systems requiring physical linkage of adjacent blocks have been designed and deployed as well (Hayley, et al., 1987; Leidersdorf, et al., 1988; Munday and Bricker, 1987). Previous authors have described linked concrete mat systems in detail and suggest its promise for both Arctic and non-Arctic applications (Hayley, et al., 1987; Leidersdorf, et al., 1988; Munday and Bricker, 1987). The objective of this paper is to describe the results of on-going performance monitoring of linked concrete mat systems deployed upon a man-made island in the rigorous Arctic offshore environment. We wish to place particular emphasis upon recent observations that indicate performance liinitations of existing concrete mat technology when subjected to the combined effects of severe Arctic wave and ice impacts at offshore deepwater sites.

Accurate range estimation is the cornerstone of modern airborne situational awareness. To determine the distance between a target and your own aircraft, we employ a sophisticated cross-correlation technique: we cross-correlate the delayed transmitted signal, $s(t)$, with the received signal, $r(t)$, where $t$ represents the internal delay and $2t$ denotes the round-trip time to the target.

In theory, the cross-correlation peak occurs precisely at the range equal to $2t$, calculated as the distance between the target and the own aircraft. In our extensive simulation experiments, peak locations may exhibit minor variations due to measurement noise and the specific phase coding scheme employed. Within the ADS-B radar system, the transmitted signal $s(t)$ is phase-modulated ADS-B. By continuously cross-correlating the received signal with multiple delayed replicas of the transmitted signal, the number of distinct peaks above a predetermined threshold directly indicates the number of detected targets. Furthermore, accurate range calculations are derived from these measured delay times.

However, correctly associating ranges with their corresponding targets remains a challenging problem [24, 25]. This complexity arises when sensors are positioned only a few meters apart, potentially causing returned echoes from different targets to arrive at the sensors in the same sequence, creating ambiguity in target identification.
